items.title: Rules of the Small Claims Court
items.says: The main goal of the Small Claims Court Rules is to let the court reach a just, quick and least expensive decision of every case on its merits. The court applies the rules liberally to promote that goal, and the parties must help it do so.

source.expect: just, most expeditious and least expensive determination

review.problem: The first sentence (the rules set out forms, steps and deadlines for every case) is not in r. 1.03, which states only the primary objective and the duty to promote it.

items.title: Small Claims Court is a branch of the Superior Court
items.says: The Small Claims Court is a branch of the Superior Court of Justice. The Chief Justice of the Superior Court is its president, and every Superior Court judge is also a judge of the Small Claims Court.

source.expect: continued as a branch of the Superior Court of Justice

review.problem: Section 22 says who the court consists of (the Chief Justice and designated Superior Court judges); who may hear and decide a case (deputy judge, Administrative Judge) is s. 24(2), not s. 22.

items.title: Who hears Small Claims cases
items.says: A Small Claims case is heard and decided by one Superior Court judge, or instead by a deputy judge appointed under section 32 or by the Small Claims Court Administrative Judge.

source.expect: a deputy judge appointed under section 32

review.problem: The gloss that a deputy judge is a lawyer appointed to the role comes from s. 32, not s. 24(2), which only names a deputy judge appointed under section 32.

items.title: Cases are decided in a summary way
items.says: The court decides all questions of law and fact in a summary (simpler, faster) way and may make any order that is just and agreeable to good conscience.

source.expect: in a summary way all questions of law and fact

items.title: Who may represent a party
items.says: A party may act for themselves or be represented by a person the Law Society Act allows, such as a lawyer or licensed paralegal. The court may exclude an unlicensed representative who is not competent to act.

source.expect: a person authorized under the Law Society Act

items.title: Rules do not allow unauthorized representatives
items.says: Nothing in the Small Claims Court Rules lets the court allow someone to act as a representative if the Law Society Act does not authorize them.

source.expect: not authorized to do so under the Law Society Act

items.title: When a representative stops acting
items.says: A representative who stops acting for a person must tell the court in writing the person's last known address, phone number and email address.

source.expect: shall notify the court in writing

items.title: Evidence rules in Small Claims Court
items.says: The court may accept and rely on any spoken testimony, document or thing that is relevant, even if it would not be allowed in another court, but not privileged material or evidence another law makes inadmissible. It may leave out evidence that is unduly repetitious.

source.expect: any oral testimony and any document or other thing

items.title: Copies of documents as evidence
items.says: A copy of a document may be accepted as evidence if the judge is satisfied that it is authentic.

source.expect: if the presiding judge is satisfied as to its authenticity

items.title: Small Claims Court fees regulation
items.says: Ontario Regulation 332/16 sets the fees paid to the Small Claims Court clerk for steps in a case, such as filing a claim, a defence or a motion.

source.expect: payable to clerks of the Small Claims Court

review.problem: Section 1(2) covers only fees payable to clerks; bailiff fees are in s. 2 and witness allowances in s. 3 of the regulation.

items.title: Monetary limit and appeal limit regulation
items.says: Ontario Regulation 626/00 sets the highest amount that can be claimed in Small Claims Court, which is $50,000.

source.expect: The maximum amount of a claim in the Small Claims Court

review.problem: Section 1(1) sets only the maximum claim amount; the appeal limit is in s. 2 of the regulation.

items.title: Limitations Act, 2002
items.says: The Limitations Act, 2002 sets the deadlines for starting most court cases in Ontario, including Small Claims Court cases.

source.expect: a proceeding shall not be commenced in respect of a claim

items.title: Gaps in the rules
items.says: If the Small Claims Court Rules do not cover a matter well enough, the court may give directions, decide by comparison with the rules and the Courts of Justice Act, and may look to the Rules of Civil Procedure.

source.expect: by reference to the Rules of Civil Procedure

items.title: Orders may include terms
items.says: When the court makes an order under the rules, it may add any terms and directions that are just.

source.expect: may impose such terms and give such directions as are just

items.title: Mistakes in following the rules
items.says: Not following a rule is an irregularity. It does not automatically cancel the case or a step, and the court may allow corrections on just terms.

source.expect: is an irregularity and does not render

items.title: Court may excuse compliance with a rule
items.says: If necessary in the interest of justice, the court may excuse a party from following any rule at any time.

source.expect: may dispense with compliance with any rule at any time

items.title: How to count days
items.says: To count a time period, leave out the first day and include the last day. If the last day falls on a holiday (including a Saturday or Sunday), the period ends on the next day that is not a holiday.

source.expect: excluding the first day and including the last day

items.title: What counts as a holiday
items.says: For the rules, a holiday includes every Saturday and Sunday and listed public holidays such as New Year's Day, Family Day, Good Friday, Easter Monday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, Civic Holiday, Labour Day, Thanksgiving, Remembrance Day, Christmas and Boxing Day.

source.expect: any Saturday or Sunday

items.title: Motion to lengthen or shorten a time
items.says: The court may lengthen or shorten any time set by the rules or by an order, on just terms.

source.expect: may lengthen or shorten any time prescribed

items.title: Changing a time by consent
items.says: A time for serving or filing a document may be lengthened or shortened by filing the parties' consent.

source.expect: by filing the consent of the parties

items.title: Use of the court forms
items.says: The forms named in the rules must be used where they apply, with changes as needed. They are listed in the Table of Forms and posted at ontariocourtforms.on.ca.

source.expect: www.ontariocourtforms.on.ca

items.title: Form 1A: Additional parties
items.says: If a form does not have room on the first page for all the parties, the rest are listed in Form 1A, attached right after the first page. Form 1A.1 does the same for extra debtors on enforcement forms.

source.expect: the remaining parties shall be listed in Form 1A

items.title: Form 15B: Affidavit
items.says: Where the rules allow or require an affidavit and no other form is named, Form 15B may be used.

source.expect: Form 15B may be used for the purpose

items.title: Filing online (outside Toronto)
items.says: Outside the City of Toronto, documents may be filed or issued through the Small Claims Court Submissions Online Portal if the portal allows it and the person accepts its terms and gives an email address for court documents. A filing counts only once the clerk confirms it.

source.expect: Small Claims Court Submissions Online Portal

items.title: Filing online in Toronto
items.says: In cases started or continued in the City of Toronto, documents may be filed or issued through the Ontario Courts Public Portal. A filing counts only once the clerk, sheriff or bailiff confirms it.

source.expect: issuance electronically through the Ontario Courts Public Portal

items.title: Case Center for Toronto hearings
items.says: Unless the court directs otherwise, in Toronto cases the documents for each hearing or conference are uploaded to Case Center. Uploading there is not filing or service.

source.expect: shall be uploaded to Case Center

items.title: Electronic filing after hours
items.says: A document filed or issued electronically outside regular business hours is treated as filed or issued on the next day that is not a holiday.

source.expect: outside of regular business hours is deemed to have been filed

items.title: How hearings are attended
items.says: A step that requires the parties to attend is held in person or by video. Telephone is allowed only for a terms of payment hearing, settlement conference, motion or trial management conference. The court may direct which method is used.

source.expect: By telephone conference, but only in the case

items.title: Request to change how someone attends (Form 1B)
items.says: A party may ask to change the way they, their representative or a witness attends a step by serving and filing a request in Form 1B with reasons, at least 30 days before the hearing date.

source.expect: at least 30 days before the hearing date

items.title: Form 1C: Objection to a change in attendance method
items.says: A party may object to a Form 1B request by serving and filing an objection in Form 1C no later than seven days after being served with the request. The court then grants, refuses or changes the method, considering things like facilities, fairness to fact-finding and illness.

source.expect: no later than seven days after being served with the request

items.title: What Small Claims Court can hear
items.says: Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money where the amount claimed is not more than the set limit, not counting interest and costs, and a claim to get back personal property worth no more than that limit.

source.expect: exclusive of interest and costs

items.title: The $50,000 limit
items.says: The most that can be claimed in Small Claims Court is $50,000. A deputy judge may also preside over claims up to $50,000.

source.expect: maximum amount of a claim in the Small Claims Court is $50,000

items.title: Deputy judge limit
items.says: A deputy judge may not decide a claim for more than the set amount, which is $50,000.

source.expect: over which a deputy judge may preside is $50,000

items.title: No splitting a claim
items.says: One cause of action cannot be split into two or more cases to fit each part under the Small Claims Court limit.

source.expect: shall not be divided into two or more actions

items.title: Superior Court needs leave for small claims
items.says: A case within Small Claims Court's jurisdiction cannot be started in the Superior Court of Justice without that court's leave, given as the rules of court provide.

source.expect: except with leave of the Superior Court of Justice

review.problem: The exception for counterclaims, crossclaims and third party claims is in CJA s. 23(1.2), not the cited s. 23(1.1).

items.title: Test for leave to sue in Superior Court
items.says: The motion for leave to start a small-claims-sized case in the Superior Court may be made without notice, and leave is granted only if it is in the interest of justice.

source.expect: only if it is in the interest of justice

items.title: Costs when a small amount is won in Superior Court
items.says: If a plaintiff in the Superior Court recovers an amount within Small Claims Court's limit, the court may order that the plaintiff recovers no costs.

source.expect: the plaintiff shall not recover any costs

items.title: Moving a Superior Court case to Small Claims Court
items.says: A Superior Court case may be moved to Small Claims Court by the local registrar, with all parties' consent filed before trial, if it only claims money or personal property and fits within Small Claims Court's limit. It then continues as if it started in Small Claims Court.

source.expect: with the consent of all parties filed before the trial

items.title: Case started in the wrong court
items.says: A case or step brought in the wrong court may be transferred or adjourned to the proper court and continued there.

source.expect: may be transferred or adjourned to the proper court

items.title: Vexatious litigant orders
items.says: If a person who is subject to an order under subsection 140(1) of the Courts of Justice Act starts or continues a Small Claims case without the order being cancelled or leave being granted, the court must stay or dismiss the case. Any party may ask for that order in writing, and it may be made without notice.

source.expect: subsection 140 (1) of the Courts of Justice Act

review.problem: Rule 12.03 does not say who makes a vexatious-litigant order or what it does; that is s. 140(1) of the Courts of Justice Act, which is not the cited provision.

items.title: Where to start the case
items.says: A case must be started in the territorial division where the cause of action arose or where any defendant lives or carries on business, or at the court location nearest to where any defendant lives or carries on business.

source.expect: in which the cause of action arose

items.title: What a territorial division is
items.says: A territorial division is a county, district or regional municipality, or one of the listed areas such as the City of Ottawa, City of Toronto or City of Hamilton.

source.expect: a county, a district or a regional municipality

items.title: Moving the trial to another place
items.says: A case is tried where it was started, but the court may order it tried elsewhere if the balance of convenience substantially favours that place. A judge who finds the case was started in the wrong place may move it to a proper place.

source.expect: balance of convenience substantially favours

items.title: Two-year limitation period
items.says: Unless the Act says otherwise, a case cannot be started after the second anniversary of the day the claim was discovered.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered

items.title: When a claim is discovered
items.says: A claim is discovered on the earlier of: the day the person first knew of the loss, that it was caused by an act or omission, that it was the other person's act or omission, and that a court case was an appropriate way to fix it; or the day a reasonable person in their situation ought to have known those things.

source.expect: the day on which the person with the claim first knew

items.title: Presumed knowledge on the day of the event
items.says: A person is presumed to have known about the claim on the day the act or omission happened, unless they prove otherwise.

source.expect: shall be presumed to have known of the matters

items.title: Loans and debts payable on demand
items.says: For a debt payable on demand, the loss happens on the first day the debtor fails to pay after a demand for payment is made.

source.expect: once a demand for the performance is made

items.title: Time does not run for minors
items.says: The two-year period does not run while the person with the claim is a minor and has no litigation guardian for the claim.

source.expect: does not run during any time in which the person with the claim

items.title: Time does not run while incapable
items.says: The two-year period does not run while the person with the claim cannot start a case because of a physical, mental or psychological condition and has no litigation guardian for the claim. (Cite s. 7(2) separately for the presumption of capacity.)

source.expect: physical, mental or psychological condition

review.problem: The presumption of capacity is in s. 7(2), not the cited s. 7(1).

items.title: Time stops during agreed mediation
items.says: If both sides agree to have an independent third party resolve the claim or help resolve it, the limitation periods stop running from the agreement until the claim is resolved, the process ends, or a party withdraws.

source.expect: agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim

items.title: Acknowledging a debt restarts the clock
items.says: If a person acknowledges liability for a fixed sum of money (or for getting back personal property), the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of the acknowledgment. Section 13 sets the rules for when an acknowledgment counts.

source.expect: acknowledges liability in respect of a claim for payment of a liquidated sum

items.title: 15-year ultimate limitation period
items.says: No case can be started more than 15 years after the day the act or omission happened, even if the claim was discovered later, subject to the exceptions in the Act.

source.expect: after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission

items.title: No limitation period to enforce a court order
items.says: There is no limitation period for a proceeding to enforce a court order, or another order that can be enforced the same way as a court order.

source.expect: a proceeding to enforce an order of a court

review.problem: The parenthetical about needing leave to issue enforcement documents after six years is not in s. 16(1).

items.title: Agreements cannot shorten the limitation period
items.says: A limitation period under the Act applies despite an agreement to change or exclude it, except as the Act allows (for example, an agreement made after October 19, 2006 may suspend or extend the basic period).

source.expect: applies despite any agreement to vary or exclude it

items.title: Adding a party after the limitation expires
items.says: Once the limitation period against a person has expired, a claim against them cannot be pursued by adding them to an existing case. Correcting a misnamed or misdescribed party is still allowed.

source.expect: shall not be pursued by adding the person as a party

items.title: 10-day notice to a municipality (road or bridge disrepair)
items.says: A claim for damages caused by a municipality's failure to keep a highway or bridge in repair cannot be brought unless, within 10 days after the injury, written notice of the claim and injury, with the date, time and location, is served on or sent by registered mail to the municipal clerk.

source.expect: within 10 days after the occurrence of the injury

items.title: Late or missing municipal notice
items.says: Missing or insufficient notice does not bar the claim if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and that the municipality was not prejudiced in its defence. Notice is not required where the injured person died from the injury.

source.expect: reasonable excuse for the want or the insufficiency

items.title: Snow and ice on municipal sidewalks
items.says: A municipality is not liable for personal injury caused by snow or ice on a sidewalk, except in a case of gross negligence.

source.expect: Except in case of gross negligence

items.title: 10-day notice to the City of Toronto
items.says: A claim against the City of Toronto for damages from a highway or bridge not kept in repair needs written notice of the claim and injury, with date, time and location, served on or sent by registered mail to the city clerk within 10 days after the injury.

source.expect: within 10 days after the occurrence of the injury

items.title: Snow and ice on Toronto sidewalks
items.says: The City of Toronto is not liable for personal injury caused by snow or ice on a sidewalk, except in a case of gross negligence.

source.expect: Except in case of gross negligence

items.title: 60-day notice for snow or ice injuries on private property
items.says: A claim for personal injury caused by snow or ice against an occupier or its snow-removal contractor cannot be brought unless, within 60 days after the injury, written notice with the date, time and location is personally served on or sent by registered mail to at least one of them.

source.expect: within 60 days after the occurrence of the injury

items.title: Late or missing snow-and-ice notice
items.says: Missing or insufficient notice does not bar the claim if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and that the defendant was not prejudiced, and notice is not required if the person died from the injury. Notice to one listed person counts against all.

source.expect: reasonable excuse for the want or the insufficiency

items.title: Car accident injury claims: 120-day notice
items.says: A claim for bodily injury or death from the use of a car is not to be started unless the plaintiff has applied for accident benefits and served written notice of the intention to sue on the defendant within 120 days after the incident (or longer if a court allows), along with other required information and steps.

source.expect: within 120 days after the incident

items.title: Effect of skipping the car-accident notice
items.says: A person may still start the case without meeting those steps, but the court must consider the non-compliance when awarding costs. No prejudgment interest is awarded for the time before the notice was served.

source.expect: may commence an action without complying

items.title: No prejudgment interest before notice (car accidents)
items.says: In a car-accident injury case, no prejudgment interest under section 128 of the Courts of Justice Act is awarded for the period before the plaintiff served the 120-day notice.

source.expect: no prejudgment interest shall be awarded

items.title: Fee to file a claim
items.says: Filing a plaintiff's claim costs $108 for an infrequent claimant and $228 for a frequent claimant (one who has already filed 10 or more claims in that office this calendar year).

source.expect: On the filing of a claim by an infrequent claimant, $108

items.title: Who is a frequent claimant
items.says: A frequent claimant is one who files a claim in an office after already filing 10 or more claims in the same office in that calendar year.

source.expect: has already filed 10 or more claims in the same office

items.title: Fee to file a defence or defendant's claim
items.says: Filing a defence costs $77. Filing a defendant's claim costs $108.

source.expect: On the filing of a defence, $77

items.title: Fee to file a motion
items.says: Filing a notice of motion (with or without notice, or for a consent order) costs $127, except a motion under the Wages Act.

source.expect: except a notice of motion under the Wages Act), $127

items.title: Fee to set a trial or assessment hearing
items.says: Fixing a date for a trial or assessment hearing costs $308 for an infrequent claimant and $403 for a frequent claimant.

source.expect: assessment hearing by an infrequent claimant, $308

items.title: Fee to request default judgment
items.says: Filing a request for default judgment costs $94 for an infrequent claimant and $128 for a frequent claimant.

source.expect: default judgment by an infrequent claimant, $94

items.title: Enforcement fees
items.says: Clerk fees: a summons to witness costs $33; a certificate of judgment $30; a writ of delivery, writ of seizure and sale or notice of examination $68; issuing or renewing a notice of garnishment $144; and preparing and filing a consolidation order $127.

source.expect: On the issue or renewal of a notice of garnishment, $144

review.problem: The last sentence about bailiff fees for each attempt comes from s. 2 of the regulation, not s. 1(2), which lists clerk fees only.

items.title: Fee to send the file for an appeal
items.says: Forwarding a court file to the Divisional Court for an appeal costs $105.

source.expect: For forwarding a court file to Divisional Court for appeal

items.title: Witness attendance money
items.says: A witness is paid $11 a day to attend court ($27 a day for a professional giving professional evidence) plus reasonable travel costs up to the kilometre allowance.

source.expect: For attendance in court, $11 per day

items.title: Fees rise with inflation
items.says: Starting January 1, 2027 and every third January 1 after, the fees are adjusted by the change in Ontario's Consumer Price Index, unless the Minister publishes a notice that a fee would exceed full cost recovery.

source.expect: Beginning on January 1, 2027

items.title: Fee waiver
items.says: A person who cannot afford court fees may ask for a fee waiver for their case. It is not available to someone acting for a business or organization. Staff decide requests that meet the income and asset limits; others may go to a judge.

source.pinpoint: Who can ask for a fee waiver
source.expect: you are not acting on behalf of a business or organization

items.title: Court fee waiver regulation
items.says: Ontario Regulation 2/05 sets out who meets the conditions for a court fee waiver: a person whose household income comes mainly from Ontario Works, ODSP, Old Age Security with the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Canada Pension Plan or a War Veterans allowance; a person whose legal aid application for the proceeding Legal Aid Ontario has approved; or a person whose household income, liquid assets and net worth are below the set limits.

source.citation: O. Reg. 2/05 (Court Fee Waivers), Administration of Justice Act
source.expect: meets the prescribed conditions referred to in subsections

review.problem: s. 2 sets who meets the prescribed conditions; it does not cover how to request a waiver or name forms FW-A-3/FW-A-4, and 'fee waiver certificate' is not in s. 2.

items.title: Litigation guardian for a plaintiff under disability
items.says: A case by a person under disability (a minor, a mentally incapable person or an absentee) must be started or continued by a litigation guardian. A minor may sue alone for up to $500.

source.expect: shall be commenced or continued by a litigation guardian

items.title: Form 4A: Consent to act as litigation guardian
items.says: A litigation guardian files a consent in Form 4A stating the disability, their relationship, that they have no conflicting interest, and that they know they may have to pay costs personally.

source.expect: file with the clerk a consent (Form 4A)

items.title: Minors suing for $500 or less
items.says: A minor may sue for any amount up to $500 as if they were an adult.

source.expect: may sue for any sum not exceeding $500

items.title: Litigation guardian for a defendant under disability
items.says: A case against a person under disability must be defended by a litigation guardian, who files a Form 4A consent with the defence. The court may appoint one if needed.

source.expect: shall be defended by a litigation guardian

items.title: Who may be litigation guardian
items.says: Any person not under disability may act, but the rules set who must act in certain cases: a parent or suitable person for a minor (or the Children's Lawyer if no one is available), a guardian or attorney for an incapable person (or the Public Guardian and Trustee).

source.expect: the Children's Lawyer shall be the litigation guardian

items.title: Setting aside a judgment against an undefended person under disability
items.says: If a case against a person under disability was not defended by a litigation guardian, the court may set aside the noting in default, any judgment and enforcement steps, on just terms.

source.expect: has not been defended by a litigation guardian

items.title: Settlements for a person under disability need court approval
items.says: A settlement of a claim by or against a person under disability does not bind that person unless the court approves it.

source.expect: without the approval of the court

items.title: Money for a person under disability is paid into court
items.says: Money owed to a person under disability under an order or settlement is paid into court unless the court orders otherwise. A motion about this money uses an affidavit in Form 4B.

source.expect: shall be paid into court, unless the court orders otherwise

items.title: Suing or being sued as a partnership
items.says: A case by or against two or more people as partners may be started using the partnership's firm name.

source.expect: may be commenced using the firm name of the partnership

review.problem: Rule 5.01 only allows a proceeding by or against partners to start in the firm name; defending in the firm name is r. 5.02.

items.title: Form 5A: Notice to alleged partner
items.says: To make an order enforceable personally against a person as a partner, the plaintiff may serve that person with the claim and a notice to alleged partner (Form 5A). That person is treated as a partner unless they defend separately denying it.

source.expect: notice to alleged partner (Form 5A)

items.title: Demand to disclose partners
items.says: In a case by or against a partnership in its firm name, any other party may serve a notice requiring the partnership to disclose the names and addresses of its partners. If it does not, its claim may be dismissed or its defence struck out.

source.expect: disclose immediately in writing the names and addresses

items.title: Suing a business name
items.says: A person carrying on business under a name other than their own may sue or be sued in that business name, and the partnership rules apply to them.

source.expect: using the business name

items.title: Enforcing against partners personally
items.says: An order against a partnership made in the firm name may be enforced against the partnership's property. (Cite r. 5.05(2)-(3) separately for enforcement against a person served under r. 5.03 who is deemed, admitted or found to be a partner, and for leave against others.)

source.expect: may be enforced against the partnership's property

review.problem: Pinpoint r. 5.05(1) covers only enforcement against partnership property; the rest comes from 5.05(2)-(3), and it turns service under r. 5.03 into one of three alternatives when it is a requirement for every person.

items.title: Plaintiff's claim (Form 7A)
items.says: A Small Claims case starts by filing a plaintiff's claim (Form 7A) with the clerk, with a copy for each defendant (no copies needed when filing online).

source.expect: filing a plaintiff's claim (Form 7A) with the clerk

items.title: What the claim must say
items.says: In plain, non-technical language, the claim gives the parties' full names, the nature of the claim with reasonable detail including the date, place and what happened, the amount and relief asked for, contact details, and the address where the defendant may be served.

source.expect: with reasonable certainty and detail

items.title: Attach the documents the claim relies on
items.says: If the claim is based on a document (such as a contract, invoice or receipt), a copy must be attached to each copy of the claim, or the claim must say why it is not available.

source.expect: a copy of the document shall be attached to each copy of the claim

items.title: Clerk issues the claim
items.says: The clerk issues the claim right away by dating, signing and sealing it and giving it a court file number. A claim filed online is issued online.

source.expect: issue it by dating, signing and sealing it

items.title: Prejudgment interest
items.says: A person entitled to an order for money may claim interest at the prejudgment interest rate from the date the cause of action arose to the date of the order, unless interest is payable another way (for example, under a contract).

source.expect: calculated from the date the cause of action arose

items.title: Postjudgment interest
items.says: Money owing under an order, including costs, bears interest at the postjudgment interest rate from the date of the order.

source.expect: bears interest at the postjudgment interest rate

items.title: Court's discretion over interest
items.says: Where it is just, the court may refuse interest, allow a higher or lower rate, or allow interest for a different period.

source.expect: where it considers it just to do so

items.title: Serve the claim within six months
items.says: A claim must be served within six months after it is issued. The court may extend this time, before or after the six months have passed.

source.expect: within six months after the date it is issued

items.title: Motion to extend time to serve the claim
items.says: A plaintiff may ask the court to extend the six-month time for serving the claim, before or after it ends.

source.expect: the court may extend the time for service

items.title: How a claim must be served
items.says: A plaintiff's claim or defendant's claim must be served personally or by an alternative to personal service set out in the rules.

source.expect: shall be served personally as provided in rule 8.02

items.title: Personal service
items.says: Personal service on an individual means leaving a copy with them. On a corporation, it means leaving a copy with an officer, director or authorized person, or a person who appears to manage a place of business. Special rules apply to municipalities, the Crown, minors and incapable persons.

source.expect: by leaving a copy of the document with him or her

items.title: Serving a municipality
items.says: Personal service on a municipality is made by leaving a copy with the mayor, chair, warden or reeve, the clerk or deputy clerk, or a lawyer for the municipality.

source.expect: with the clerk or deputy clerk of the municipality

items.title: Serving the Crown in right of Ontario
items.says: Personal service on the Crown in right of Ontario is made in accordance with section 15 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019.

source.expect: section 15 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019

review.problem: Service on the Crown in right of Ontario by email is r. 8.03(9), not r. 8.02, which only refers to section 15 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019.

items.title: Alternative service at a home
items.says: If personal service at a person's home fails, the document may be left in a sealed envelope with an adult member of the household, and another copy mailed or couriered to the home on the same or next day.

source.expect: anyone who appears to be an adult member of the same household

items.title: Alternative service on a corporation
items.says: If a corporation cannot be found at its last address on government record, it may be served by mailing or couriering a copy to the corporation at that address and to each director at their recorded address.

source.expect: to each director of the corporation

items.title: When alternative service takes effect
items.says: Service at a home or on a corporation by these alternative methods is effective on the fifth day after the document is mailed or the courier confirms delivery.

source.expect: is effective on the fifth day after the document is mailed

items.title: Service on a lawyer or paralegal
items.says: A party with a lawyer or paralegal may be served by leaving the document at their office, but only if the lawyer, paralegal or employee writes an acceptance of service and the date on it.

source.expect: endorses on the document or a copy of it an acceptance of service

items.title: Serving a claim by registered mail or courier
items.says: A claim may be served on an individual by registered mail or courier to their home, if the person or a household member signs to confirm receipt. Service is effective on the date of that signature shown in the delivery confirmation.

source.expect: by registered mail or by courier to the individual's place of residence

items.title: Motion for substituted service
items.says: If it is shown that prompt service of a claim personally or by an alternative method is impractical, the court may allow substituted service (another method it approves).

source.expect: impractical to effect prompt service of a claim

items.title: Serving a defendant outside Ontario
items.says: If the defendant is outside Ontario, the court may award as costs what was reasonably spent serving the claim there.

source.expect: costs reasonably incurred in effecting service

items.title: Serving a defence and other documents
items.says: A defence and any document not covered by a special rule may be served by mail, courier, email, personally or by an alternative to personal service, unless the court orders otherwise.

source.expect: by mail, by courier, by email, personally

items.title: Service by mail takes effect on day five
items.says: Service by mail is effective on the fifth day after mailing.

source.expect: on the fifth day following the date of mailing

items.title: Service by courier takes effect on day five
items.says: Service by courier is effective on the fifth day after the courier confirms delivery to the sender.

source.expect: courier verifies to the sender that the document was delivered

items.title: When email service takes effect
items.says: Service by email is effective on the day the email is sent, or on the next day if it is sent between 4 p.m. and midnight.

source.expect: between 4 p.m. and midnight, on the following day

review.problem: The required contents of the email are in r. 8.08(3), not the cited r. 8.08(4).

items.title: Report a change of address within seven days
items.says: A party whose address for service changes must serve notice of the change on the court and the other parties within seven days.

source.expect: within seven days after the change takes place

items.title: Form 8A: Affidavit of service
items.says: Service is proved by an affidavit of service (Form 8A) from the person who served the document. A lawyer or paralegal may instead use a certificate of service (Form 8B).

source.expect: affidavit of service (Form 8A)

items.title: Form 8B: Lawyer or paralegal's certificate of service
items.says: A lawyer or paralegal who served a document, or had it served, and is satisfied it was served may prove it with a certificate of service (Form 8B).

source.expect: certificate of service (Form 8B)

items.title: Showing a document never reached you
items.says: A person served or deemed served may still show, on a motion to set aside a default, to extend time or to adjourn, that the document did not come to their notice or came later.

source.expect: did not come to the person's notice

items.title: Defence due within 20 days
items.says: A defendant who wants to dispute the claim must, within 20 days of being served, serve a defence (Form 9A) on every other party and file it with proof of service.

source.expect: within 20 days of being served with the claim

items.title: What the defence must say
items.says: The defence states, in plain language with reasonable detail, why the defendant disputes the claim, plus contact details. Documents the defence relies on must be attached or the defence must say why they are not.

source.expect: The reasons why the defendant disputes the plaintiff's claim

items.title: Set-off as a defence
items.says: In a claim for a debt, a defendant may, as a defence, claim to set off a debt the plaintiff owes them.

source.expect: claim the right to set off against the plaintiff's claim

items.title: Admit the claim and propose a payment plan
items.says: A defendant who admits all or part of the claim may say so in the defence and propose terms of payment.

source.expect: admit liability and propose terms of payment

items.title: If the plaintiff does not dispute the proposal
items.says: If the plaintiff does not dispute the proposal within 20 days, the defendant must pay as proposed as if it were a court order. If payments are missed, the plaintiff may serve a notice of default of payment (Form 20L) and, after 15 days, file an affidavit of default (Form 20M) for judgment on the unpaid balance.

source.expect: as if it were a court order

items.title: Plaintiff disputes the payment proposal within 20 days
items.says: The plaintiff may dispute the proposed terms of payment within 20 days after service of the defence by filing and serving a request to clerk (Form 9B) for a terms of payment hearing.

source.expect: within 20 days after service of the defence

items.title: Terms of payment hearing
items.says: The clerk sets a hearing before a referee or other person, who may order terms of payment. An individual defendant receives a financial information form (Form 20I), completes it and serves it on the creditor but does not file it.

source.expect: may make an order as to terms of payment

items.title: Defendant misses the terms of payment hearing
items.says: If the defendant does not appear, the clerk may sign default judgment for the admitted part of the claim.

source.expect: for the part of the claim that has been admitted

items.title: Missed payments under a terms of payment order
items.says: Unless the order says otherwise, if the defendant misses payments, the clerk signs judgment for the unpaid balance when the plaintiff files an affidavit about the default.

source.expect: the clerk shall sign judgment for the unpaid balance

items.title: Form 9B: Request to clerk
items.says: A request to the clerk (Form 9B) is used to ask the clerk to fix a trial date. Once a settlement conference has been held and the fee is paid, the clerk fixes the date and serves a notice of trial.

source.expect: request to the clerk (Form 9B)

review.problem: Rule 16.01(1) mentions Form 9B only as the request to fix a trial date; its use to note default, request an assessment hearing or a terms of payment hearing comes from other rules (11.01, 11.03, 9.03).

items.title: Defendant's claim (Form 10A)
items.says: A defendant may make its own claim against the plaintiff, or against another person if the claim arises from the same transaction or occurrence or is related to the plaintiff's claim.

source.expect: arising out of the transaction or occurrence relied upon by the plaintiff

items.title: Defendant's claim within 20 days of the defence
items.says: The defendant's claim (Form 10A) may be issued within 20 days after the defence is filed, or later but before trial or default judgment with the court's leave.

source.expect: within 20 days after the day on which the defence is filed

review.siteCorrection: The stage map counted this 20 days from the first defence filed by any defendant.
